title: Gods You Carry, a God Who Carries
overview: The chapter contrasts Babylon's idols, which must be hauled around like cargo, with Israel's God, who says he has carried his people from birth and will carry them into old age.

parts.label: Babylon's gods hauled away (vv. 1-2)
parts.note: Bel (a title for Marduk, Babylon's chief god) and Nebo (his son, god of writing) were normally paraded in grand processions. Here the poem pictures their statues loaded onto tired pack animals like baggage, unable to save themselves as Babylon falls.

parts.label: The God who carries (vv. 3-4)
parts.note: Speaking to the surviving exiles of Israel, God turns the picture around: idols must be carried, but he has carried his people since they were born. He promises to keep carrying and rescuing them, even when they are old and gray.

parts.label: Making a god for hire (vv. 5-7)
parts.note: The poem mocks the process of idol making: people pay out gold and silver, hire a craftsman, then bow to what he produces. Once set in place the statue cannot move, answer or help anyone in trouble.

parts.label: Remember who said it first (vv. 8-11)
parts.note: God addresses the rebels among his people, telling them to remember his past acts and claiming to announce outcomes long before they happen. The 'bird of prey from the east' is generally understood as Cyrus, the Persian king named earlier in Isaiah, who would conquer Babylon swiftly.

parts.label: Rescue is close (vv. 12-13)
parts.note: God tells the stubborn, who are far from righteousness, that his rescue is near and will not be delayed. 'Righteousness' in verse 13 means God doing right by his promises, which is why it is paired with salvation for Zion, meaning Jerusalem.

think: What in your life do you feel you have to keep carrying, and is there anything you feel carries you?
